text.p: To open a book shop here with nothing but Philippine titles would have been financial suicide a few years ago, but a resurgence of nationalistic pride among Filipinos has made it one of the best-sellers in town.
"We're doing so well. We're so happy with the way we're doing that we want to set up two or three more as soon as possible," said Jose Maria Lorenzo Tan, owner of The Filipino Bookstore.
The rekindling of national pride, which has brought success to Tan, has also been in evidence in the run-up to Thursday's celebrations of the 99th anniversary of independence.
Weeks before the event, government buildings as well as houses and cars were adorned with the Philippine flag, something never seen in the past.

Living under 400 years of Spanish rule and 45 years of U.S. domination subdued the national identity and deepened a sense of inferiority that prompted Filipinos to buy Western and shun local traditions.
The situation has so alarmed the country's leaders that they are encouraging a revival of nationalism ahead of the 100th anniversary of independence in 1998.
One of the first measures was the Filipinisation of the education system, where the national language Filipino was introduced as the medium of instruction in place of English.
But change is taking time and the language of the government and business remains English. FLOURISHING LOCAL BOOK INDUSTRY
Karina Bolasco, assistant general manager of Anvil Publishing, which is one of the biggest publishers in the country, said sales of Filipino books had risen sharply in recent years.
"Whereas before it would take two to three years to sell a thousand copies of a local book, right now, we can sell 3,000 copies in just one year," she said.
Among Anvil's best-sellers is a book on young heroes who fought and died for freedom during the dark days of martial rule under Ferdinand Marcos, who was ousted in 1986.
"There is a greater awareness and consciousness on anything Filipino," Bolasco added.
Local publishers produced more than 3,500 titles in 1995, up from a mere 1,000 titles in the previous year.
Other arts have also benefited from the wave of nationalism. RENAISSANCE OF VISUAL ARTS
Art galleries that sprouted around Manila are exhibiting new works of contemporary Filipino artists almost every week.
"There is some kind of a renaissance in Philippine art," said Silvana Diaz, owner of Galleria Duemila in Manila.
She said there was a movement of artists who stressed "Filipino-ness" in their work.
Non-traditional art media too have joined in the bandwagon.
A novelty shop selling T-shirts proclaiming "Pilipino Ako" -- "I'm a Filipino" -- now has a chain of stores competing head-on with foreign brands.

National Centennial Commission chairman Salvador Laurel said the renewed sense of nationalism in recent years was more deeply rooted than was felt after the 1986 popular revolt which toppled the Marcos regime.
The sense of unity right now is not born out of hatred against a reviled regime, but rather a sense of hope for the future of the country.

The centennial commission, which will orchestrate the pomp and pageantry of the 100th year of Philippine independence in 1998, has re-introduced Filipino martyrs and heroes to instill patriotism among Filipinos.
"We are aiming for something more longer lasting. We want something to remain -- the rekindling of the spirit of our heroes and martyrs," Laurel said.
